hooks.text: Earth fills just 0.12 of a single pixel.
Is the sunbeam in the Pale Blue Dot real?
4 billion miles away, Earth became 0.12 of a pixel.

title: Earth Fills Just 0.12 of One Pixel
description: The true story behind the Pale Blue Dot reveals that the iconic sunbeam was actually an optical artifact inside the camera.

beats.text: Earth fills just 0.12 of a single pixel.
beats.visual: Cropped version of the Pale Blue Dot showing the tiny pixel of Earth, 1990

beats.text: In nineteen ninety, Voyager 1 looked back from approximately 4 billion miles away to snap a final portrait of home.
beats.visual: Illustration of the Voyager 1 spacecraft at the edge of the solar system

beats.text: Astronomer Carl Sagan pushed for the photo, but NASA resisted because a single pixel had no scientific value.
beats.visual: Photograph of astronomer Carl Sagan in the 1980s

beats.text: The probe captured sixty frames of our solar system, including giants like Jupiter and tiny specks like our own.
beats.visual: The Voyager 1 Family Portrait mosaic showing multiple planets, 1990

beats.text: The most famous shot shows Earth suspended in a dramatic, celestial-looking beam of golden light.
beats.visual: The full Pale Blue Dot image showing the ray of light across the frame, 1990

beats.text: That ray wasn't space magic; it was just sunlight bouncing inside the lens and glinting off the camera hardware.
beats.visual: Illustration of sunlight reflecting inside the Voyager 1 camera optics

beats.text: Engineers then powered the cameras down forever, leaving the probe to drift into the interstellar dark.
beats.visual: A Deep Space Network antenna at the Goldstone Observatory

beats.text: It is our most distant perspective of home, where Earth fills just 0.12 of a single pixel.
beats.visual: The 2020 NASA remaster of the Pale Blue Dot
